t.1.145.1: Janamejaya said: Having gone to Ekacakrā, those sons of Kuntī, the great chariot-warriors, what did the Pāṇḍavas do after that, O best of the twice-born?
t.1.145.2: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having gone to Ekacakrā, those sons of Kuntī, great chariot-warriors, dwelt for a short time in the house of a brāhmaṇa.
t.1.145.4: Then all of them went about seeking alms, O lord of the people, and by their own virtues they became pleasing to behold in the eyes of the townsfolk.
t.1.145.3: Seeing lovely forests of many kinds, as well as the regions of the earth, the rivers, and the lakes,
t.1.145.5: And every night they would present the alms to Kuntī, and they would eat the portions divided by her, each one separately.
t.1.145.6: Those heroes, scorchers of their foes, eat one half together with their mother, while Bhīma of great strength eats the other half of all the alms.
t.1.145.7: And while those great-souled ones were dwelling there thus, O king, a very long time then passed, O bull of the Bharatas.
t.1.145.8: Then one day those bulls among the Bharatas went out for alms, but Bhīmasena, as it happened, stayed there with Pṛthā.
t.1.145.9: Then, O Bhārata, Kuntī heard a great and terrible cry, born of distress, rising loudly in the house of the brāhmaṇa.
t.1.145.10: Out of compassion and her goodness of heart, O king, the queen could not bear to see them all wailing loudly and lamenting.
t.1.145.11: Then the noble Pṛthā, her heart as if churned by sorrow, spoke these words full of compassion to Bhīma.
t.1.145.12: We are living very happily, son, in the brahmin's house, unknown to the Dhārtarāṣṭras, honored and free from sorrow.
t.1.145.13: Son, I am always thinking: what kindness might I do for this brahmin, such as those who have dwelt happily in a house would do in return?
t.1.145.15: Surely this sorrow has befallen this brahmin. If we could give him help in this matter, it would be a good deed.
t.1.145.14: This much is the measure of a man, dear son: that a kindness done to him is never lost, and that whatever another may do for him, he should do still more in return.
t.1.145.16: Let it be found out what this man's sorrow is and from what cause it has arisen. Once it is known, I shall resolve to act, even if it should be very hard to do.
t.1.145.17: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: And as the two of them were conversing thus, they heard once more, O lord of the people, a cry born of distress from that brahmin and his wife.
t.1.145.18: Then Kuntī hastily entered the inner apartments of that great-souled brahmin, like a cow whose calf is tied up.
t.1.145.19: Then she saw that brahmin there, together with his wife, his son and his daughter, his face distorted with grief.
t.1.145.21: In life there is the greatest sorrow, in life there is the greatest fever; for one who abides in life, the coming of the pairs of opposites is certain.
t.1.145.20: Fie on this life in the world, whose essence is fire, which is without purpose, rooted in sorrow, dependent on others, and full of what is unpleasant!
t.1.145.23: Some say that liberation is the highest goal, yet it is in no way attainable; and in the gaining of wealth, hell in its entirety indeed arises.
t.1.145.22: For even a man who stands alone cannot pursue dharma, artha and kāma; and separation from these is also held to be the greatest sorrow.
t.1.145.24: The craving for wealth is the greatest misery; in the gaining of wealth there is more misery still; and for one who has grown attached to wealth, its loss brings misery greater yet.
t.1.145.25: For I see no means by which I might be freed from this calamity, or by which I might flee to safety together with my son and wife.
t.1.145.27: "I was born here and have grown up here, and my father too is here": this is what you said, foolish woman, when I entreated you again and again.
t.1.145.26: Indeed, I made an effort before, as you know, O brāhmaṇī, to go wherever there was safety, but you did not listen to me.
t.1.145.28: For your aged father has long since gone to heaven, and so has your mother, and your kinsmen too belong to the past. What delight, then, is there in living there?
t.1.145.29: Because you, longing to stay near your kinsfolk, would not listen to my word, this ruin of my family has now come upon me, causing me bitter grief.
t.1.145.30: Or rather, let this be my own destruction, for I shall not be able to abandon any kinsman and myself go on living like a cruel man.
t.1.145.31: Her who shares my dharma, self-controlled, ever like a mother to me, this friend appointed for me by the gods, ever my highest refuge.
t.1.145.33: You, my wife, well-born and endowed with good character, the mother of my children, virtuous, never doing me harm, and ever devoted to me, I shall not be able to abandon for the sake of my own life.
t.1.145.34: How could I myself ever bring myself to abandon my daughter, a young girl who has not yet come of age, whose form does not yet bear the marks of womanhood?
t.1.145.32: Having duly chosen her, who was appointed for me by my mother and father and is ever my partner in household life, and having wedded her with the sacred mantras,
t.1.145.35: She is a pledge entrusted to me by the great-souled Creator for the sake of her future husband, and through her I hope, together with my ancestors, to attain the worlds won by a daughter's sons. Having begotten that young girl myself, how can I bring myself to abandon her?
t.1.145.36: Some men think that a father's affection for his son is greater, but by no means for his daughter; to me, however, both are regarded as equal.
t.1.145.37: How can I bring myself to abandon that sinless young girl, in whom the worlds and offspring are ever happily established?
t.1.145.39: To abandon any one of these would be cruel, and the wise condemn it; yet if I abandon myself, these will die without me.
t.1.145.38: And even if I give up my own self, I shall be tormented once I have passed into the power of the dead; for, clearly, abandoned by me, these will not be able to live here.
t.1.145.40: I, such as I am, have fallen into dire straits and am unable to cross this calamity. Alas, shame! What course shall I take today, together with my kin? Death together with all of them is better, but life is not fitting for me.
